To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the crystallography models may be unstable upon extended refinement against the experimental data and that this instability is caused by insufficiently restrained model geometries.

(i) crystallographic refinement may appear unstable at higher and at lower resolution; (ii) at higher resolution the instability is caused by the relatively small fraction (~5%) of disordered atoms in the model; and (iii) at lower resolution the instability is due to insufficiently strong geometry constraints.
the crystallography model may appear to divergently refine in the presence of a relatively small number of disordered atoms, or when insufficiently strong geometric restraints are applied.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of crystallographic model refinement and the identification of the possible sources of refinement instability.
the apparent instability of crystallography refinement in the presence disordered model fragments, and upon insufficiently strong restraints on the model geometry.
the problem of the convergence of crystallography refinement and the stability of resulting models.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
crystallographic refinement of macromolecules is not an exact process.
the crystallography of biological macromolecules is still a very young science.
crystallographic refinement should be performed with the most restrained model geometry, but at the highest resolution possible, to avoid the risk of model instability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the crystallography refinement is an inherently ill-posed problem and that the refinement results should be interpreted with care.
crystallographic refinement of macromolecular models may be unstable in the presence of model fragments that are not well defined and in the absence of sufficient restraint geometry.
the crystallography community should be cautious in interpreting the results of crystallographic model building and refinement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is essential for the refinement protocol to include the appropriate restraints on the model geometry, especially at lower resolution, and to avoid the use of disordered model components.
crystallographic models may be refined to a state that is not stable with respect to small perturbations.

crystallographic refinement of macromolecular models should always be performed with the highest possible resolution and with a sufficient number of restraints to prevent the model from becoming unstable upon refinement.
